Appendix B Many-Body Density of States of Disordered Solids

This appendix connects assumption (2.35) to experiment, particularly the temperature dependence of specific heat Cv​(T)C_{v}(T). We also find the density of states the many-body density state of amorphous solids in closed form.

The amorphous specific heat, as found from experiment is,

Cv​(β)=aβ.C_{v}(\beta)=\frac{a}{\beta}.

The average energy is related to the partition function as

U=−∂βlogZ\displaystyle U=-\partial_{\beta}\log Z (B.1)

Since the specific heat of glasses are linear in temperature, the UU must have the form,

U=a​T2+b=aβ2+bU=aT^{2}+b=\frac{a}{\beta^{2}}+b

At zero temperature the block is in its ground state, which we (arbitrarily) chose to be zero. Thus

b=0.b=0.

Then from eqn(B.1),

Z=A​ea/β\displaystyle Z=Ae^{a/\beta} (B.2)

Here the constant A is the degeneracy of the ground state. This is because

limβ→∞Z=limβ→∞∑ne−β​En\lim_{\beta\rightarrow\infty}Z=\lim_{\beta\rightarrow\infty}\sum_{n}e^{-\beta E_{n}}

is equal to number of states for which EnE_{n} is exactly equal to zero. We can now find the density of states f⁡(E)f(E) from

Zβ=∫0∞f⁡(E)​e−β​E​𝑑EZ_{\beta}=\int_{0}^{\infty}f(E)e^{-\beta E}dE

by substituting eqn(B.2) on the lhs and expand both the partition function and the density of states,

A​ea/β=A⁡(1+aβ+…)=∫0∞[f(1)​(E)+f(2)​(E)+…]​e−β​E​𝑑E.Ae^{a/\beta}=A(1+\frac{a}{\beta}+\ldots)=\int_{0}^{\infty}[f^{(1)}(E)+f^{(2)}(E)+\ldots]e^{-\beta E}dE.

The first term of the left hand side can be obtained if

f(1)​(E)=A​δ​(E),f^{(1)}(E)=A\delta(E),

whereas the second can be obtained if

f(2)​(E)=a​A.f^{(2)}(E)=aA.

This way we can get f⁡(E)f(E) up-to all orders. The result is,

f⁡(E)=A⁡[δ⁡(E)+S⁡(E)]f(E)=A[\delta(E)+S(E)]

where

S⁡(E)=∑n=1∞En−1​ann!​(n−1)!.\displaystyle S(E)=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{E^{n-1}a^{n}}{n!(n-1)!}. (B.3)

One may ask why there is a delta function in the density of states. This is because, for ϵ\epsilon close the level spacing, the integral

∫−ϵϵf⁡(E)​𝑑E\int_{-\epsilon}^{\epsilon}f(E)dE

must give AA, the number of levels at E=0E=0, consistent with our choice of E0E_{0} and eqn(B.2). Let’s look at for which value of n is the most prominent in eqn(B.3). We will assume that k≫1k\gg 1, since these are the typical energies accesible to experiment.

Sk=log⁡[ck​Ek−1k!​(k−1)!]=k​log⁡c+(k−1)​log⁡E−log⁡k!−log⁡(k−1)!S_{k}=\log\left[\frac{c^{k}E^{k-1}}{k!(k-1)!}\right]=k\log c+(k-1)\log E-\log k!-\log(k-1)!

Using Stirling’s approximation, log⁡k!=k​log⁡k−k+1\log k!=k\log k-k+1

log⁡Sk=k⁡(log⁡c+log⁡E)−log⁡E−k​log​k+2​k−3−k​log⁡(k−1)+log⁡(k−1).\log S_{k}=k(\log c+\log E)-\log E-k\log k+2k-3-k\log(k-1)+\log(k-1).

differentiating with respect to kk and setting it to zero, we find

k⁡(k−1)=c​E.k(k-1)=cE.

Thus, at energy EE, the term k≈c​E≫1k\approx\sqrt{cE}\gg 1 dominates the density of states.

Sc​E=2​c​E−2S_{\sqrt{cE}}=2\sqrt{cE}-2

One can find a closed form for f⁡(E)f(E) by using an asyptotic form of the modified bessel function of the first kind, Iν​(z)I_{\nu}(z). For z≫1z\gg 1, we can approximate

I1​(z)≈ez2​π​zI_{1}(z)\approx\frac{e^{z}}{\sqrt{2\pi z}}

since the density of states can be written in terms of this special function

f⁡(E)=A⁡[c​I1​(2​c​E)E+δ⁡(E)]\displaystyle f(E)=A\left[\frac{\sqrt{c}I_{1}(2\sqrt{cE})}{\sqrt{E}}+\delta(E)\right] (B.4)

we can simplify

f⁡(E)≈A​c1/4​e2​c​E81/4​π1/2\displaystyle f(E)\approx Ac^{1/4}\frac{e^{2\sqrt{cE}}}{8^{1/4}\pi^{1/2}} (B.5)

This asymptotic form of the modified bessel function of the first kind is well known. It is derived from a saddle point approximation, by writing

∑kSk≈∫Sk​𝑑k=∫eln​Sk​𝑑k\sum_{k}S_{k}\approx\int S_{k}dk=\int e^{\mbox{ln}{S_{k}}}dk

and expanding ln​Sk\mbox{ln}S_{k} at its sharp peak up to second order.

Appendix C Author’s Biography

Dervis Can Vural was born on January 10, 1982, in New Brunswick, New Jersey. He received his B.Sc. degree in Physics from Middle East Technical University in Turkey, in 2002 and his M.S degree in Physics from the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign in 2004.
